articles.title: After arriving in the US with $500, former tennis player Andres Bernal began investing in Connecticut real estate in 2016; a decade later, he says he owns more than 60 rental units worth over $12 million
articles.summary: When Andres Bernal arrived in the United States with $500, his immediate goal was not to build a real estate empire.
articles.body: When Andres Bernal arrived in the United States with $500, his immediate goal was not to build a real estate empire. The Dominican-born former professional tennis player had come to pursue the sport he had played since childhood. But after years of teaching tennis and working long hours, he began looking for a different route to financial independence.Real estate, a concept he had first encountered through his family in the Dominican Republic, eventually became that route. His first investment came in 2016. Nearly a decade later, Bernal says his Connecticut portfolio has grown to more than 60 rental units valued at over $12 million, states a podcast interview published by Harbordise Partners.From tennis courts to property sealsBernal's introduction to real estate began long before his first investment. His godfather was a builder in the Dominican Republic, and Bernal had watched him acquire and develop property while growing up.After playing professional tennis for nearly two years in the US, Bernal began teaching the sport, sometimes working 50 to 60 hours a week. Looking for a way to build income beyond trading time for money, he started studying stocks, businesses and real estate, states the interview. He eventually focused on property investing, learning the fundamentals before making his first investment in 2016.The strategy has since expanded beyond long-term rentals. Bernal completed more than 50 property flips during 2024 and 2025, building a business around acquisitions, renovations and sales while continuing to grow his rental portfolio.A portfolio built around different tenantsAccording to the video interview, his Connecticut holdings include multifamily properties, duplexes, single-family homes and student rentals. Some properties operate through the federal Section 8 housing program, while others serve traditional tenants. Student housing has become an important part of the portfolio. Bernal owns properties near three Connecticut universities and typically rents homes to groups of students whose parents or family members co-sign their leases. Keeping properties within walking distance of campuses is another central part of the strategy, reducing the need for parking and transportation.His Section 8 properties provide another source of rental income, although they come with additional inspections and administrative requirements. Bernal says he has about 22 units connected to the program.Building the business behind the propertiesManaging dozens of properties and completing frequent flips requires more than finding deals. Bernal has built a network of contractors and property-management support to keep the operation moving. His flipping operation includes about a dozen contractors handling work such as carpentry, painting and basic plumbing and electrical tasks. A smaller part-time team manages the rental portfolio. That structure allows the same network of workers to move between renovation projects and maintenance needs, reducing the need to constantly find new contractors.Knowing when to hold and when to sellBernal's approach has also evolved with the performance of individual properties. He and his partners have sold some older Connecticut properties where substantial equity was tied up but cash flow no longer justified holding them. His renovation philosophy follows a similar hierarchy. Safety, structural problems and major mechanical issues come first, followed by improvements that can increase rental value and appeal. Cosmetic upgrades come later when the numbers support them.For Bernal, the bigger lesson from a decade in real estate has been discipline. Deals need to be conservatively underwritten, renovation budgets need room for surprises, and projected resale values cannot be treated as guarantees.What began with $500 and a career on the tennis court has evolved into a Connecticut real estate business spanning rentals, student housing, affordable housing and property flips.Images Courtesy: Facebook and istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Angela Scanlon to take over Sara Cox's drivetime slot on Radio 2
articles.summary: The station also announces a new presenter for its country show after Bob Harris's departure.
articles.body:
Angela Scanlon is to take over BBC Radio 2's drivetime show after Sara Cox moved to the breakfast slot.

The Irish personality said it was "properly exciting" to be hosting the station's 16:00-19:00 show every weekday from November.

She said: "Millions of people, all having completely different days, piling into the same conversation for a few hours - what a strange and lovely thing!"

Scanlon, who hosted a Sunday early morning programme on the station from 2018 to 2021, was among a number of people who filled in after Cox vacated the drivetime slot in May, including Joel Dommett, Jason Manford, Ellie Taylor, Alex Jones and Gary Davies.

Scanlon is also known for The One Show, This Morning, Your Home Made Perfect, The Apprentice: Unfinished Business, and for taking part in Strictly Come Dancing in 2023.

"Every weekday, I'll be in your ears, your cars and your kitchens - on the school run, on the way home, or standing at the hob wondering what on earth to feed a small but hungry mob," she said.

"I want all of it: the stories, the opinions, the chaos, the tiny triumphs and the things you probably shouldn't admit on national radio."

Radio 2 controller Helen Thomas described Scanlon as "incredibly warm and quick witted and proved to be extremely popular with the Radio 2 audience this summer".

She added: "Drivetime is such an important show in terms of ensuring people get home and start their evenings in a positive and upbeat mood, and I'm delighted Angela will be taking up the reins in November.

"I'd like to extend my thanks to all the hosts who have presented in this slot since our Sara moved on up to Breakfast."

Scanlon also hosted the Virgin Radio weekend breakfast show after Graham Norton's departure in 2024, and co-hosts the Get A Grip podcast.

Meanwhile, Radio 2 has also announced that Ben Earle will present the station's weekly country music programme following the departure of longtime host Bob Harris.

"Whispering" Bob, who presented the show for 27 years, announced his departure in June, weeks after revealing his prostate cancer has spread to his spine.

Earle, one half of British country group The Shires, has also fronted a weekly show on Absolute Radio Country for the past five years.

Thomas said: "His knowledge, passion and enthusiasm for the genre, coupled with his years as a musician plus experience presenting on the radio, make him the ideal person to pick up the reins from the legendary Bob Harris. Like Bob, I hope Ben hosts the show for decades to come."

articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who himself has an arrest warrant by International Criminal Court, has asked an inter-ministerial team to
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who himself has an arrest warrant by International Criminal Court, has asked an inter-ministerial team to prepare a potential case for ICC against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan over Turkey’s treatment of Kurds and alleged support for Hamas.According to the report by i24NEWS, Netanyahu instructed an inter-ministerial team and the director of Israel’s International Law Department to begin preparing the case.The report said the proposed legal action would focus primarily on Erdogan’s treatment of Kurdish minorities in Turkey, while also examining allegations related to Turkish government funding and support for Hamas.Netanyahu himself is subject to an ICC arrest warrant issued in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.The ICC said there were reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu was criminally responsible for alleged acts including starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution and other inhumane acts. Netanyahu and Israel have rejected the allegations and challenged the court’s jurisdiction.The reported move comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ankara and Tel Aviv, with both governments increasingly turning to international legal and diplomatic mechanisms against each other.i24NEWS said the preparation of the case could also be linked to Turkey’s efforts to pursue action against Netanyahu through international channels.The report also said Israeli officials hoped the case might not ultimately need to be filed, with the threat of potential legal action being considered as a deterrent against further Turkish moves. Netanyahu’s office and Israel’s Justice Ministry declined to comment on the report.Turkey faces criticism over treatment of KurdsTurkey’s conflict with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) began in 1984 and has killed more than 40,000 people over four decades.Human rights groups have for years criticised Ankara over its treatment of Kurdish politicians and activists. Human Rights Watch said in its 2026 report that Turkey had yet to take steps to ensure equal rights for Kurds, amend what it described as abusive counterterrorism laws or release Kurdish political prisoners.It also highlighted the continued imprisonment of former pro-Kurdish HDP leaders Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ.The criticism also extends to local politics. Human Rights Watch and other rights groups have documented the removal of elected Kurdish mayors and their replacement by government-appointed trustees, while the European Parliament has criticised the practice as undermining local democracy.Turkey maintains that its counterterrorism measures are aimed at the PKK and other groups it considers security threats, rather than Kurds as an ethnic community. articles.title: My 999 call foiled RAF Fairford plot, farmer tells BBC
articles.summary: The member of the public says the authorities "dropped the ball" in their handling of the incident.
articles.body:
A farmer who told the BBC her 999 call "foiled" a suspected terror plot says police and security services "dropped the ball" in their handling of the incident.

She told BBC News she called police just after 01:30 BST on Sunday after seeing three vans parked in a "weird formation" near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. The vans had a "large group of hooded and masked men" outside who started to "panic" when they saw her.

Five men, all UK nationals from London in their early to mid 20s, have been arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Breakfast he was grateful to the local resident but that she had only "a partial picture".

Streeting said of the farmer: "I do want to thank the member of the public who acted quickly and called this in.

"I would also just say, respectfully, that she has a partial picture.

"And I won't go beyond that, in terms of commenting on operational security matters."

The local resident from Whelford, who wanted to remain anonymous, said she was coming home from a party when she found the road and her driveway blocked by three white vans.

She described the vans as having "strange signage" on them.

"I looked at it and thought 'that is not real'," she told BBC News.

"When they saw me, they then ran ahead of me, some into the field and some into the neighbouring village of Kempsford.

"I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place."

The farmer was aware that RAF Fairford was operating at a high security level so immediately called the Ministry of Defence police, but did not receive an answer.

She then called 999 at 01:36, and said that within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police.

She also revealed that hours before her encounter, her neighbour had phoned her "in tears" after she had tried to drive home at about 20:00 BST on Saturday and was stopped by armed personnel.

The woman said she remained "staggered by the whole story".

"This sort of thing doesn't happen," she said. "I still can't process how that base, on high alert, how this has happened.

"I think it was pure luck that I arrived in the village at a similar time to the vans.

"I'm absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this."

She added: "The airbase were operating a roadblock close to the entrance to the base, but not on any of the other roads.

"We assumed someone would be monitoring the roads around the base perimeter and taking regular patrols in the village, clearly this was not happening.

"I believe my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had."

She added she was surprised the roads around the base were not being monitored and the village was not evacuated of residents until 06:00.

"I think they were hyper focused and vigilant about the the base itself and had absolutely no regard for our village," she said.

"The vans were within metres of houses and those people were left unaware.

"I'm just really keen to highlight that it appears someone really dropped the ball on this."

She also said it was "strange" that police said they had received reports of suspicious vehicles approaching the base nearly an hour before her call.

Of her neighbour's encounter on Saturday night, the farmer said: "She was stopped outside the main gates of the airbase. It was armed American personnel. They were incredibly aggressive.

"She had her children in the car, and they made them all put their hands out of the car, shouted at her to put her car in neutral.

"She was really upset. And in the end, they had to turn round. They couldn't drive that way to their own house."

Other villagers have spoken to BBC News about what they saw happening around the base in the days leading up to the arrests.

One reported seeing a man jumping out of some bushes wearing a backpack early on Friday, while a dogwalker said they were told by armed police to return home and stay indoors on Saturday afternoon.

Responding to Streeting's comments about her having a "partial picture" of what had happened, the farmer added: "I don't know how he knows what picture I've got. I've never met him.

"Literally nobody in any sort of official capacity has been in touch with me or anyone else in the village."

The police cordon around the area remains in place and local residents are yet to return home.

The defence secretary told BBC Breakfast more than 80 homes had been evacuated.

He added he was fairly limited in what he could say about the incident but that an investigation was "well under way".

He said he understood it was frustrating for the public that he could not share more information - but it was "a small price to pay" to protect the integrity of the police and security services.

US President Donald Trump said the US, which uses RAF Fairford as a forward operating location for "defensive" strikes on Iran, had the men "under view for a long time, and we got them".

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects" speculation linking the country to the arrests of the five men.

Streeting went on to issue an "enormous thank you" to local members of the public for showing "vigilance" and "forbearance".

He also thanked the police, security services and counter terror police for how they handled the incident.

The five men who were arrested under the Explosives Act and on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act remain in custody.

Gloucestershire Constabulary's Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth confirmed the force had made the initial arrests but that Counter Terror Police were leading the investigation.

articles.title: Russia strikes Ukraine's largest mobile service provider; why communication networks matter in war
articles.summary: Russia struck the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest mobile service provider, in Kyiv on Sunday, in the latest attack on the country’s
articles.body: Russia struck the headquarters of Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest mobile service provider, in Kyiv on Sunday, in the latest attack on the country’s communications infrastructure. Kyivstar confirmed that its head office was hit and said there were no casualties.According to Reuters, the strike came as Moscow continued attacks on Ukrainian data centres and communications infrastructure.Russia’s defence ministry said it had struck a Vodafone Ukraine data centre, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Kyiv data centre was hit twice, wounding two children and an adult.Russia had already been stepping up strikes on Ukraine’s data centres and telecommunications infrastructure in the days before the Kyivstar attackOn September 23, Russian strikes damaged facilities used by several internet providers in Kyiv, disrupting internet services for around 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to Ukraine’s digital transformation ministry.According to Ukrainian companies and officials, infrastructure belonging to providers including Domonet, Kievnet and Faust was damaged, while a data centre housing infrastructure for hosting provider MiroHost was destroyed. A Russian strike also damaged a Datagroup data centre in Kyiv, further disrupting Ukraine’s digital infrastructure.Russian defence ministry said the strikes included data-processing and telecommunications centres such as New-Telco and United DC, claiming they were linked to Ukrainian military communications and intelligence. Moscow also said the Datagroup facility was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.Why Ukraine’s communications network matters in the warUkraine’s communications infrastructure has become an increasingly important part of its war effort, connecting military units, command centres and battlefield systems while also carrying information used for air-raid and missile alerts.Ukraine foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia was targeting major Ukrainian data centres in an attempt to disrupt the flow of information, while stressing that rapid missile and drone alerts are crucial for saving lives.As the war has become increasingly dependent on drones, real-time intelligence and networked command systems, reliable digital connectivity has become critical to the speed at which information moves from the battlefield to commanders and frontline forces.Ukraine’s military also relies on digital platforms to build a real-time picture of the battlefield. Systems such as Delta combine information from multiple sources to help commanders track Russian forces, monitor battlefield developments and coordinate operations

articles.title: Michael Mann’s former Hollywood Hills home has sold for $3.5 million after repeated price changes; the 3,002-square-foot Villa Hillside, built in 1929, had been listed several times over the past two years
articles.summary: Perched above the Sunset Strip, Villa Hillside has spent the past two years moving in and out of the Los Angeles luxury market, with its asking price
articles.body: Perched above the Sunset Strip, Villa Hillside has spent the past two years moving in and out of the Los Angeles luxury market, with its asking price repeatedly changing along the way. The 3,002-square-foot Hollywood Hills residence, once owned by filmmaker Michael Mann, has now found a buyer for $3.5 million, closing another chapter in the property's unusually eventful sales history, states an online report by California Luxury Homes. Built in 1929, the four-bedroom, four-bathroom home sits across two contiguous parcels totaling roughly 11,700 square feet. Its combination of Mediterranean-inspired architecture, mature landscaping and sweeping views gives it a distinctly secluded character despite its location minutes from some of Los Angeles' busiest neighborhoods, states the report.A Hollywood pedigree of its ownMann, known for films including Heat, Collateral, Miami Vice and Ferrari, was the property's original owner, according to its marketing materials. That connection adds an unmistakable piece of Hollywood history to a residence that otherwise feels deliberately removed from the city's entertainment industry. Villa Hillside was designed by architect Daniel Romualdez, whose work has been recognized by Architectural Digest, while landscape designer Sarita Jaccard shaped the gardens. Racing Green is also credited with construction. The architecture favors warmth over spectacle. Cream-colored plaster walls, dark wood floors, French doors and arched openings give the interiors a Mediterranean character, while the surrounding gardens soften the transition between house and hillside.A private screening room hidden in plain sightThe report adds that one of the property's most distinctive details is tucked inside the main living room. A concealed projection screen can descend in front of the room's large picture window, turning the space into a private screening room while allowing the Los Angeles view to remain the focal point when the screen is raised.The formal dining room continues the home's traditional aesthetic, with an elongated table and olive-green velvet chairs. An adjoining breakfast nook sits beneath an archway near the kitchen, which features gray shaker cabinetry, white countertops, stainless-steel appliances and arched windows. Upstairs, the primary suite centers on a sculpted plaster fireplace and opens toward a private balcony. Its adjoining bathroom features pale stone, a double vanity, arched detailing and a deep soaking tub incorporated into an open shower area. Two additional bedrooms occupy the upper floor, continuing the restrained combination of white plaster, wood flooring and dark-framed windows.The hillside becomes part of the houseOutside, Villa Hillside's relationship with its terrain becomes even more apparent. A raised wood deck steps into the slope, surrounded by succulents and drought-tolerant planting before descending toward the pool and entertaining areas, adds the report. The pool terrace includes built-in seating, a dining area and a rectangular fire pit. A dark-bottom pool and spa sit beside pale paving and a cascading water wall, giving the outdoor area the feel of a compact private resort. A secluded outdoor bathing area adds another unusual feature: a freestanding claw-foot tub tucked among tropical greenery on a small wooden platform.A long and winding path to $3.5 millionThe latest sale follows a series of price changes. Villa Hillside was marketed for $4.595 million in February 2025, later appearing at $4.499 million and $3.95 million before reaching $3.55 million in October. By March 2026, the asking price had fallen to $3.35 million, followed by another listing at $2.5 million in April. The property then changed hands for $2.6 million on June 2. That was not the final transaction, however. Villa Hillside returned to the market in July, eventually selling for $3.5 million on September 15, 2026. Based on its reported living area, the latest sale works out to roughly $1,166 per square foot.Above the Sunset StripThe home's location remains one of its strongest features. Set in the Hollywood Hills, it offers quick access to the Sunset Strip, West Hollywood, Beverly Hills and Hollywood while retaining the privacy and elevated views associated with hillside living. Its mature landscaping and carefully arranged outdoor spaces make the property feel larger than its 3,002 square feet suggest. Rather than relying on enormous interiors, Villa Hillside builds its appeal around views, architecture, gardens and the connection between indoor and outdoor spaces. With its latest $3.5 million sale, the 1929 residence has completed one of the more unusual recent journeys through the Hollywood Hills market. Its Michael Mann connection adds a layer of cinematic history, but the house ultimately stands on its own as a secluded hillside retreat above Los Angeles.Images Courtesy: California Luxury HomesReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: US 81-year-old viral delivery driver's $700K fundraiser for wife's cancer treatment pulled after discovering daughter posed as neighbour to raise money
articles.summary: A Texas couple's $700K GoFundMe fundraiser for cancer treatment was pulled after it was revealed the organizer was their daughter posing as a neighbor. Discover the shocking details and the family's new appeal for help.
articles.body: A fundraiser that collected more than $700,000 for a Texas couple has been removed after GoFundMe found that the campaign organiser had falsely presented herself as a neighbour.The appeal was created for 81-year-old Donald Johnson, a viral delivery driver who gained attention after footage showed him delivering lost luggage while working to help pay for his wife Josephine’s cancer treatment.The campaign launched on September 2 and was taken down after GoFundMe received a tip on September 25 questioning the identity of the person behind it, NewsNation reported.GoFundMe's Trust & Safety team found that the organiser, who had identified herself as a neighbour named “Erin Howell”, was actually the couple's daughter, Amy Johnson.“Our Trust & Safety team identified factual misrepresentations, which directly violate our Terms of Service,” GoFundMe told NewsNation.Amy told the platform that she had used the neighbour persona because she believed the family's circumstances would resonate more strongly with donors if the appeal came from someone outside the family.She said footage showing her father delivering luggage had been provided by a neighbour who wanted to remain anonymous. Amy maintained that the video was genuine and that the other details in the fundraiser, including her father's work, her mother's cancer diagnosis and the family's financial difficulties, were accurate.GoFundMe said that misrepresenting an organiser's identity or relationship with the beneficiary breaches its terms regardless of the organiser's intentions. The platform removed the campaign and refunded all donations.“Taking action like this allows GoFundMe to protect donors’ generosity and our continued ability to support people who are fundraising to help others,” the company said.Johnson began delivering lost luggage as an independent contractor about three years ago after his wife was diagnosed with an aggressive form of pancreatic cancer, according to the family.The 81-year-old said he regularly worked 14-hour days and drove hundreds of miles to support his wife.After the GoFundMe campaign was removed, Amy created a new fundraiser for her parents on GiveSendGo on Saturday, according to NYP.In the new appeal, she acknowledged the controversy surrounding the original campaign while maintaining that the family's circumstances had not changed.“My mom has pancreatic cancer. The bills are high. My dad is 81 and still works delivering luggage so they can stay afloat,” Amy wrote.She also said the neighbour who provided the doorbell footage was real and that the video, her mother's diagnosis and her father's job were genuine.“A lot of you already gave on GoFundMe. We are so grateful. That page was originally set up on my account because it was already established and we thought that would be the simplest way,” she wrote.GoFundMe, however, said Amy acknowledged during a recorded call that she had posed as a neighbour when setting up the original campaign.The new fundraiser had collected more than $45,000 towards its $100,000 target as of Monday.Amy said the family had restarted the appeal so that people who still wanted to help could contribute directly.“We started over on a new page so your support can actually reach them this time,” she wrote.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Against EVMs even if we win all seats': Akhilesh, Mayawati express distrust, cite US, Germany
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and BSP supremo Mayawati on Monday questioned the use of electronic voting machines (EVMs), with both
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and BSP supremo Mayawati on Monday questioned the use of electronic voting machines (EVMs), with both leaders calling for greater voter confidence in the electoral process.Yadav said the Samajwadi Party would oppose EVMs even if it won "all seats" in an election. Questioning the need for multiple layers of technology in voting, he pointed to countries such as the US and Germany, which he said use ballot papers."Why is there a need for a machine after a machine?" he asked at a press conference at the party headquarters."We have already told you that even if we win all the seats, we are against EVMs," Yadav said.He also questioned whether the US uses ballot papers despite India's ties with Washington. Citing Germany as another example, Yadav said the country had not adopted EVMs despite being advanced in technology and research.Mayawati, meanwhile, said voters must be confident that their votes cannot be diverted or counted in favour of another candidate. She said any such doubt could undermine public faith in the democratic system.“It is crucial that the voter harbours no doubt that their vote might have been diverted to or counted for another candidate; such an occurrence would effectively amount to the murder of democracy and would destroy the people's faith in the democratic system,” news agency ANI quoted her as saying.Mayawati recalled that ballot papers were used for several decades after India's first election before EVMs were introduced. She also pointed to the BJP's earlier opposition to EVMs when the Congress was in power, saying the party had alleged that the machines were being misused.“However, surprisingly, after winning the election and forming the central govt, the BJP did not abolish EVMs; instead, it has continued the practice of voting and counting via these very machines,” she said.The remarks came amid a wider political debate over the Election Commission and its handling of electoral rolls, including the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. The Election Commission has rejected suggestions that reported objections raised by election commissioners over aspects of the SIR process amounted to institutional dissent, saying inputs and suggestions during the draft stage are part of its regular decision-making process.Yadav also said the SP had already worked out its strategy against the BJP and claimed voters would remove the party from power."We have already made our strategy to remove the BJP. And without removing the BJP, you cannot remove anyone. The real crisis is the BJP. Once the BJP is removed, all institutions will be fine," he said."The BJP will be removed on its own. articles.title: Pakistanis turned to rooftop solar as power bills soared; it has now saved $12 billion in fuel imports
articles.summary: The global solar capacity is growing rapidly, so much so that by 2030, approximately 100 million households will rely on rooftop solar, according to the
articles.body: The global solar capacity is growing rapidly, so much so that by 2030, approximately 100 million households will rely on rooftop solar, according to the International Energy Agency. According to research by the World Economic Forum, covering only about 50% of the world's existing rooftops with solar panels could meet total global electricity demand. One such country that has taken a massive step in this direction is Pakistan.Over the past few years, Pakistan has adopted solar power at rates that have saved it billions during an ongoing global energy crisis. It has even cushioned the country from the effects of the war going on in Iran, which has impacted much stronger economies massively.Pakistan gets almost all of its oil and gas from the Middle East, where US and Israeli bombing of Iran has caused crude prices to jump past $150 a barrel and tankers to be stuck in the Strait of Hormuz for months. While it might still be spending on fuel imports, the country has saved much in electricity due to a recent yet rapid shift to solar power.It was at the beginning of the Ukraine War that the country began its solar boom, when it couldn't afford to buy liquefied natural gas, leading to power outages. “It also led to soaring electricity bills,” said Rabia Babar, an energy market analyst at the Pakistan-based nonprofit Renewables First, as per a report by Fast Company.Some power bills were as much as 30-40% of people's income, more than they were spending on accommodation. According to WEF, Pakistan's electricity bills have spiked by a whopping 155% since 2021. At the same time, the price of solar panels had fallen steeply about 60% in a year, and an oversupply of them was available in the country from Chinese manufacturers. Thus, people naturally shifted to buying and installing, in order to avoid using grid power.“You could go to your local bodega, buy a solar panel and charge controller and a battery, and install it yourself,” said Jigar Shah, an energy entrepreneur and investor who previously led the Loans Program Office at the U.S. Department of Energy, to the outlet. “It was so cheap that people were able to do it with discretionary funds, $50 that they had.”What followed then was a grassroots DIY movement. Self-taught solar entrepreneurs learned about installation and repair of the panels on YouTube and local WhatsApp groups. As one installed solar on their roofs, the neighbours followed. Businesses added solar and batteries to factory buildings. Farmers started using solar pumps, rather than diesel, for irrigation. Cheap solar panels also helped bring power to rural homes that had always been off the grid.In 2025, Pakistan was the second-largest importer of Chinese solar panels in the world. Driven by small installations across the country, about ten per cent of the grid shifted to solar within a few years. “When you think about the sheer volume and the population of Pakistan, it certainly is the largest deployment of solar and battery storage to solve energy poverty in the world,” Shah said.Over the past decade, Pakistan has imported a massive 51 gigawatts of solar power. That’s more than the entire capacity of power plants on the country’s electric grid. This slow and steady yet impactful move has helped the country avoid spending more than $12 billion on fossil fuel imports, according to a report from Renewables First.While it still has to import fossil fuels for transportation, the solar power dependence could save another $6.3 billion in the country's pockets as crude prices surge even further. According to the World Resources Institute, Pakistan is undergoing "one of the most striking people-led energy shifts in history."What makes the entire transition interesting is that the shift to solar power in Pakistan was a people's solution to a problem, rather than a government-driven programme. Often shifts to green energy are slow and led by policy, but in Pakistan it has been rapid and spontaneous due to a combination of market forces and citizen initiative.You use AI every day. articles.title: Apple ordered to pay $5.7bn in haptic tech patent case
articles.summary: Audio firm Taction Technology claimed Apple infringed its patents for tech used to power device vibrations.
articles.body:
Apple has been ordered to pay $5.7bn (£4.3bn) in damages after a US jury found it had used another firm's tech without permission.

Audio firm Taction Technology claimed in 2021 that Apple had infringed two of its patents for haptics systems, which enable vibrations for actions such as receiving a message or pressing a button.

This tech is built into devices like the iPhone and Apple Watch.

Apple said it had not used Taction's vibration tech and would appeal the verdict.

"While we thank the jury for their consideration, we strongly disagree with today's verdict and the damages awarded, which are entirely unsupported by the facts," it said.

"Apple's Taptic Engine is fundamentally different from Taction's technology, which Taction's own testing of Apple's products confirmed during trial."

Haptics allow people to interact with devices by simulating the sense of touch or feel through vibrations.

They have become a hallmark of modern devices, with smartphones, watches and video game controllers among those containing small motors that move in response to specific electronic signals.

Apple's "Taptic Engine" system - enabling haptic feedback in its devices - first debuted with the Apple Watch in 2014.

Since then, it has improved its underlying system, and with that expanded haptics in its devices.

Taction, which makes headphones and gaming headsets, claimed in 2021 that these improvements infringed patents it was issued in 2020.

It wrote in its complaint that by producing better haptic vibrations in its devices, Apple had been able to improve its overall user experience.

As such, the tech giant had been "capitalising on Taction's innovation and success by selling devices that infringe [its] patents", Taction said.

It also accused Apple of using its inventions "without license or authority".

A San Diego judge ruled in 2023 that Apple did not infringe upon Taction's patents.

However, an appeal was subsequently taken up by a federal appeal circuit - resulting in a September jury trial at the US District Court for the Southern District of California which found in its favour.

In Friday's verdict , jurors did not find that Apple had infringed the patents in question willingly.

It marks one of many similar lawsuits the tech giant has defended itself against in recent years.

In November 2025 a judge ordered Apple to pay $634m to medical tech firm Masimo after a jury found it had infringed a patent for blood-oxygen reading tech.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The home ministry on Monday directed the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) to abolish all 34 sanctioned posts of its security wing at Swami Ramdev's Patanjali Food and Herbal Park Pvt Ltd in Haridwar, ending the sanctioned manpower structure of the deployed wing.The force had withdrawn its security from the premises on May 4. articles.title: Since 2006, the African Water Facility has backed 148 projects; its programmes have improved water access for 23.2 million people
articles.summary: Since 2006, the African Water Facility has provided grants and other support for 148 water and sanitation projects across Africa.
articles.body: Since 2006, the African Water Facility has provided grants and other support for 148 water and sanitation projects across Africa. The facility says those projects have improved access to water supply for 23.2 million people, provided sanitation access to 11.3 million people and equipped 2 million hectares with irrigation. It has provided €220 million in grants and helped mobilise €2.1 billion in downstream investment, according to the African Development Bank. The figures were highlighted at a water and sanitation investment event during the bank's 2025 Annual Meetings in Abidjan, as the facility prepared to enter a new 2026-2030 strategy period. The programme's work spans project preparation, investment planning and support for water and sanitation infrastructure, with its financing designed to help projects move towards implementation.How the African Water Facility prepares water and sanitation projectsThe African Water Facility is a project preparation fund focused on water and sanitation in Africa. It provides grants, technical assistance and investment support to governments and works with partners on water projects. The facility is an initiative of the African Ministers' Council on Water and is hosted and managed by the African Development Bank. Although the facility was established in 2004, it became operational in 2006, when it funded its first project to support the creation of the Volta River Basin Authority.Since 2006, the facility says it has provided €220 million in grants across 148 projects and mobilised €2.1 billion in downstream investment. Its current pipeline was valued at €90 million in the figures presented at the 2025 Annual Meetings and was expected to benefit 15 African countries. The facility's role is concentrated on project preparation, helping governments develop projects and strengthen the conditions needed to attract larger sources of financing. At the May 2025 Annual Meetings event, African water-sector officials and experts also discussed project bankability, financing mechanisms, private-sector participation and partnerships as continuing challenges for the sector.What the facility's projects have deliveredThe figures reported by the African Development Bank cover several parts of the water sector. The facility says its projects have improved access to water supply for 23.2 million people and provided sanitation access for 11.3 million people. They have also equipped 2 million hectares with irrigation. These figures describe the cumulative results reported for projects supported by the facility since 2006.The wider health implications of water, sanitation and hygiene are documented in independent research. A 2023 study published in The Lancet, titled Burden of disease attributable to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene in domestic settings: a global analysis for selected adverse health outcomes, estimated that 1.4 million deaths and 74 million disability-adjusted life-years could have been prevented through safe water, sanitation and hygiene in 2019 across four health outcomes examined by the researchers. The study estimated that 69% of diarrhoea, 14% of acute respiratory infections and 10% of undernutrition were attributable to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene under its methodology. The figures were global estimates for 2019 and were not specific to projects supported by the African Water Facility.Research has also examined the relationship between sanitation and education. A 2017 systematic review titled Effects of sanitation on cognitive development and school absence: A systematic review identified 17 studies. It found some evidence of an association between household sanitation and improved cognitive outcomes, but rated the overall evidence as having poor methodological quality, while findings on school absence were mixed and uncertain. Another 2017 study, Sanitation and Education, published in the American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, found that school latrine construction substantially increased enrolment among pubescent-age girls, particularly when sex-specific latrines were provided. The study also found benefits for younger children, while noting that latrine construction did not increase academic test scores.The African Water Facility's new 2026-2030 strategyThe facility's next phase is set out in its 2026-2030 strategy, which places greater emphasis on preparing investment-ready projects, mobilising financing and expanding partnerships. The strategy identifies project preparation as a central priority and calls for high-quality, bankable project pipelines capable of attracting larger downstream financing. It also places emphasis on innovative and blended financing approaches, private-sector engagement and institutional capacity.The strategy also includes a stronger focus on sanitation. The Africa Urban Sanitation Investment Initiative, or AUSII, operates as a dedicated urban sanitation financing window within the African Water Facility. Its stated objective is to increase the scale and impact of investment in urban sanitation by helping create financing options and an enabling environment for projects. The initiative has been piloted in seven countries: Uganda, Kenya, Zambia, Ghana, Mauritania, Côte d'Ivoire and Togo. Its work includes developing sanitation master plans, investment planning, inclusive on-site sanitation and faecal sludge management.AUSII was created to address the financing and preparation of urban sanitation projects, with the facility describing bankable project development and catalytic investment as part of its approach. The initiative's longer-term targets include preparing 50 sanitation projects and providing 15 million people in African urban areas with access to safely managed sanitation and hygiene services. It also aims to mobilise additional commercial and concessional finance for sanitation projects.The African Water Facility entered the 2026-2030 strategy period with a focus on expanding the number of projects that can move from preparation to implementation and attracting additional sources of financing. Its record since 2006, measured through 148 supported projects, 23.2 million people with improved water supply access, 11.3 million with sanitation access and 2 million hectares equipped with irrigation, provides the baseline for that next phase.You use AI every day. articles.body: In February 2026, the Florida Department of Environmental Protection announced the largest conservation easement in Florida Forever's 25-year history, protecting 61,525 acres of working forestland in Baker and Union counties, providing permanent habitat connectivity for species including the bald eagle, red-cockaded woodpecker and eastern indigo snake. The DEP identifies the bald eagle, red-cockaded woodpecker and eastern indigo snake among the species supported by the property.The protected land includes forested wetlands, floodplain forests, basin swamps and headwaters. The agency said the river basins are increasingly important as regional communities continue to grow.Why will the protected land remain in active forest managementThe easement does not remove the land from forest management. Conserving this single-owner tract in perpetuity strengthens landscape-scale connectivity while allowing the land to remain in active forest management that supports the local economy.”Weyerhaeuser’s Director of Conservation, Alex Littlejohn, also described the agreement as an opportunity to maintain both habitat and working forestland. “Environmental stewardship is fundamental to our operations, and this conservation easement was a unique opportunity to support wildlife habitat and connectivity at a huge scale while also continuing to support the local forest economy,” Littlejohn said, according to the DEP.Governor recommends $115 million for Florida ForeverThrough the Florida Forever Program, the state conserves land that provides environmental, recreational and preservation benefits, according to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). articles.title: Getty acquired a rediscovered 17th-century Velázquez portrait in Los Angeles; the painting, known for centuries only through an engraving, is now the first work by the Spanish master to enter the museum’s collection
articles.summary: The J.
articles.body: The J. Paul Getty Museum has acquired a long-lost 17th-century portrait by Spanish painter Diego Velázquez, bringing the first work by the Baroque master into the museum’s permanent collection. The oil painting, titled Portrait of the Count-Duke of Olivares, was officially announced by the Los Angeles museum on 23 September 2026. Before its recent discovery in a private European collection, art historians knew the image only through a famous 17th-century engraving by Flemish printmaker Paulus Pontius, created in collaboration with Peter Paul Rubens. It is the first Velázquez painting held by a museum on the West Coast of the United States. The work will go on public display at the Getty Center’s East Pavilion in Los Angeles before traveling to Michigan for a museum exhibition next year.First Velázquez painting for Getty collectionThe acquisition fills an important gap in the Getty Museum’s collection. Until now, the museum had no works by Velázquez, despite its large collection of European art. "Velázquez was one of the greatest painters of early modern Europe and one of the most remarkable proponents of the long and multifaceted tradition of state portraiture," said Timothy Potts, director of the Getty Museum. "This work is a landmark addition to Getty's collection, made even more extraordinary by the painting's history as it was not fully known until recently." There are around 120 known surviving paintings by Velázquez worldwide, with about 50 held by the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid. Davide Gasparotto, senior curator of paintings at the Getty Museum, described the canvas as an important addition to the museum’s collection of early European art. "This commanding and almost intimidating portrait is a strong visual record of one of Spain's most powerful 17th century statesmen that exemplifies the painter's innovation in court portraiture and his superb ability to capture the sitter's personality directly from life," Gasparotto said. "It is a major addition to the Getty's collection of 17th-century European paintings and adds a major example to our growing holdings of Spanish paintings."Subject of near absolute powerMeasuring 60 by 48 centimetres, the bust-length canvas shows Gaspar de Guzmán y Pimentel, the Count-Duke of Olivares. Wearing gold-trimmed armor and a red sash, Olivares turns his head and looks directly at the viewer. During the 1620s and 1630s, Olivares served as valido, or prime minister, to King Philip IV of Spain. For more than two decades, he held near absolute power over decisions involving the Spanish government, administrative reforms, and military operations. Velázquez likely painted the work in the summer of 1626 as a diplomatic gift for Cardinal Francesco Barberini, who was visiting Madrid on a papal mission. Historical records support this idea. An inventory of the Barberini family collection in Rome from 1631 lists "a painting with the portrait of Count Olivares, that is [his] head and armored bust." Experts believe this description refers to the Getty painting.Centuries of hidden ownershipAfter reaching Italy in the 17th century, the painting stayed in private hands for centuries. It was eventually held by the Coppellotti family collection in Asti, northern Italy, throughout the 20th century. The painting passed to a private collector in 2025 before being purchased by the Getty Museum. For generations, art historians knew the composition only through an engraving by Paulus Pontius. The print was made in collaboration with Peter Paul Rubens. Rubens created an elaborate allegorical border around Olivares' head, while inscriptions on the print clearly said that the central portrait was based on a prototype by Velázquez. A surviving letter from Olivares to Rubens confirms that the prime minister received copies of the print and thanked the Flemish artist. The newly identified canvas has been confirmed as the original prototype Velázquez made for that print.Identification by Spanish art scholarThe painting was identified by Salvador Salort-Pons, director of the Detroit Institute of Arts and a specialist in 17th-century Spanish art. While researching an upcoming exhibition about portraits of Olivares, Salort-Pons found the unrecorded painting in a private collection. Further technical study found several pentimenti, or visible changes made by the artist directly on the canvas while working. Changes to Olivares’ armor and clothing supported the conclusion that the work was an original Velázquez painting, rather than a later copy. After its display at the Getty Center in Los Angeles, the painting will travel to the Detroit Institute of Arts. There, it will be part of the exhibition Velázquez & Olivares: Early Years at Court, scheduled to run from 24 January to 25 July 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Plan for controversial Sydney data centre scrapped after push-back
articles.summary: Goodman Group, the property giant behind the Project Mars data centre, says the decision is due to changes to the "policy and regulatory environment".
articles.body:
Plans for a data centre which would have been built metres from people's homes in a Sydney suburb have been scrapped following intense push-back by campaigners.

The data centre was being developed by Goodman Group, Australia's biggest property company, and would have seen it construct a A$1.2bn (£630m; $841m), 90-megawatt facility known as Project Mars in the Lane Cove area.

The company confirmed it was withdrawing its application in a letter to the local planning authority. It follows a concerted opposition against the data centre by local residents and campaigners.

The dispute captures a wider disagreement in Australia over the role of data centres.

With the mainstreaming of generative AI in recent years, there has been a huge swell in demand for data centres, and Australia - with its abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land - has become a global destination for their construction .

However, while the country's government has been keen to attract investment from global AI companies, there has also been stiff opposition due to the huge demands the centres place on water and energy supplies, and the disruption they cause local communities.

The proposal for Project Mars, which would have been constructed about 20 metres from the nearest house in the suburb of Lane Cove, received 374 submissions during a consultation - with just nine in support of it.

According to local news website In the Cove, this is highest number of submissions ever received for a data centre application .

In its letter to New South Wales Department of Planning, Goodman Group said since starting the planning process in March 2025, it had "undertaken extensive technical investigations, stakeholder engagement and community consultation".

"During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly," it said.

It said it had "carefully considered these changes" along with the "views of the local community", and concluded it would not proceed with the development.

The decision by Goodman Group follows an announcement by the New South Wales government last month that it would be introducing a fast-track programme for data centres.

The programme would allow them to be assessed within 75 days, provided they meet requirements around certain standards and fund the additional supply of water and energy.

In a message posted to the Facebook page of Lane Cove Responsible Planning Group, Anthony Roberts, a member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly representing Lane Cove, said it was "a huge win for the Lane Cove West community".

"This is a common-sense win for our community," he said.

"This victory sends a clear message to other data centre developers. To find suitable locations before putting proposals forward.

"Data centres have an important role to play, but developments of this size and scale need to be appropriately located and planned with the surrounding community in mind."

articles.title: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.summary: John Healey's speech comes ahead of next month's Budget, as he faces pressure to bring down government borrowing costs.
articles.body:
The chancellor has warned against allowing Britain's benefits bill to balloon while not offering young people opportunities.

John Healey told Labour's annual conference in Liverpool that cutting welfare spending was "more than an economic must - it's a moral duty".

"The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage," he said.

He announced the expansion of a Local Apprenticeships Service for mayors in England, which he said would deliver thousands more apprenticeships for young people.

Healey's speech comes as he faces pressure to cut public spending or raise taxes ahead of next month's Budget to bring down government borrowing costs.

In an attempt to reassure the markets, he said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" with him and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "united on meeting the fiscal rules".

Fiscal rules are the government's self-imposed constraints to manage decisions on spending and tax.

The Budget would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space", the chancellor said.

And he admitted that "the money New Labour had in the '90s is simply not there now".

Healey blamed the Conservative Party's time in government for leaving Britain spending more on debt than on the Home Office, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice combined.

Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said in response to the speech that "Labour MPs will never support cutting the out-of-control welfare bill" and "with Labour, it's always more taxes if you work and more benefits if you don't".

Healey praised young people as "digital natives, whip-smart, questioning, ambitious, brave" who could move from "generation jeopardy to generation hope".

But he pointed to the million young people not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - which he said created a necessity to make benefits a bridge into work, rather than a "trap".

"It is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn't offer a future," he said.

The Local Apprenticeships Service was initially planned as a pilot in a limited number of areas but would now be available to any English mayor who wants it, he said.

Through the scheme, which the Treasury says will roll out across England from March 2027, local teams plan to match young people with employers, including small businesses that have never taken on a trainee.

The department said an extra £100m was going into the scheme, "fully funded" by savings from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Powers to implement the scheme will rest with mayors because "they know which firms are hiring, which colleges are delivering, which estates have been left behind," Healey said.

It comes as the final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the one in eight people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are Neets in the coming weeks.

Healey said these young people had been "signed off, written off" which the Labour government would address.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for fiscal studies think tank, told the BBC that sticking to fiscal rules alone would not be enough to reduce debt because it is "basically a promise to get down debt tomorrow".

She suggested that reducing the benefits bill, including removing support from some people, could be one way of cutting the national debt sooner.

Elsewhere in his speech, Healey repeated his promises to re-industrialise the country and said Rolls Royce would invest £300m more into its British factories in Derby, Bristol, Glasgow and Rotherham.

He also said he was bringing back the Union Learning Fund in England, established in 1998 and abolished by the Tories, to help working people gain more skills in an age of artificial intelligence. It was initially unclear how this would be funded.

articles.summary: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei on Monday warned that foreign forces would soon be pushed out of the Arabian Sea, while asserting that
articles.body: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei on Monday warned that foreign forces would soon be pushed out of the Arabian Sea, while asserting that Iran’s armed forces and people remained prepared to confront the country’s adversaries.In a written message published by Iranian media, Khamenei said enemy forces had been driven back from waters off southern Iran and warned they would not be able to maintain their presence in the Arabian Sea."Some see us as the fourth superpower in the world. Today, the enemy's forces do not dare to venture beyond the Arabian Sea. Soon the day will come when the Arabian Sea will be purged of their presence. Our people fill the squares and streets across the country with their responsible presence," he said.The message was issued on the occasion of Iran's "Sacred Defense Week" and the anniversary of the death of Hezbollah leader Sayyid Hassan Nasrallah. It comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear programme, after US President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal linked to reopening the strategic waterway.Khamenei said different sections of Iranian society, despite their apparent differences, were united in supporting the country’s position, including its claim over the Strait of Hormuz."Presently, throughout Islamic Iran—adorned by the presence of diverse ethnicities—various declarations of readiness, particularly armed readiness, exist to construct an arena that will bring renown to them and disgrace to their enemy," he said.He also claimed that Iranian forces had inflicted losses on their adversaries in the waters around the country."The two southern seas of Iran were the roaming grounds of enemy forces. Today, however, due to the painful blows they have received from the brave warriors and guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they do not advance past the Arabian Sea. Whenever they have braved this danger, they have brought harm upon themselves—and soon, the Arabian Sea too will be cleared of them," he said.Khamenei further said that sections of Iranian society were standing together to protect what he described as their "rightful positions"."There were days when the enemy constantly tried to weaken the social backbone of the system, but nowadays, various strata of society, despite their apparent differences, stand firm on maintaining their rightful positions, including the preservation of the blessed Strait of Hormuz," he said.Khamenei’s remarks came after Washington rejected Tehran’s proposal linked to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Last week, on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined a seven-day proposal under which Iran would reopen the waterway if certain conditions were met by the US.Iran said the proposal was conveyed through intermediaries and linked the reopening to steps including easing US military pressure.On Sunday, US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz said Trump had rejected the proposal because Tehran had sought sanctions relief and access to "billions in frozen assets" before entering negotiations on its nuclear programme.Waltz said Washington would ultimately need to reach "some type of agreement" with Iran, but added that Trump would keep all "options on the table".Araghchi disputed Waltz’s account, saying the US ambassador had not seen the proposal. He also said Iran remained open to diplomacy but was prepared for renewed hostilities."We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed. We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. We don’t care about U.S. midterm elections. We care about our national interests. At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," Araghchi said in an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press".In his message, Khamenei also referred to Iran’s past confrontation with foreign powers, accusing them of attempting to weaken the country’s social and political foundations."There were days when the hegemonists, through psychological operations and creating an atmosphere of intimidation, emptied the streets of the capital and launched a coup against this nation's quest for independence, subsequently plundering the wealth of this country for 25 years," he said.He said Iranians had demonstrated their support for the country’s defence efforts over the past seven months."Yet, for the past seven months, our compatriots across the nation have adorned the squares and streets with their responsible and enthusiastic presence to warm the hearts of the warriors of Islam and cast terror into the enemy's heart," he said.Khamenei also referred to the participation of women in what he described as acts of courage, while asserting that Iran’s past circumstances would not return."This comparison between the past days and the present days can be expanded further, but in short, as a servant of the dear people of Iran, I declare that those former days—which our enemy dreams of returning to—are gone and will never recur," he said.Nasrallah was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Hezbollah’s main headquarters in Beirut’s southern suburbs on September 28, 2024. The Israel Defence Forces confirmed his death at the time, saying, "Hassan Nasrallah will no longer be able to terrorize the world."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2015, a man saw two children drinking from a puddle in Ghana and built a solar water kiosk; 10 years later, his project supplies 126M litres
articles.summary: In 2015, Sunil Lalvani witnessed two children drinking water from a puddle during a trip to Ghana, an encounter that prompted him to act.
articles.body: In 2015, Sunil Lalvani witnessed two children drinking water from a puddle during a trip to Ghana, an encounter that prompted him to act. Drawing on his background in electronics, he deployed Project Maji’s first solar-powered water kiosk, initially as a corporate social responsibility project under his family business. Ten years later, the organisation says its work has expanded far beyond that first installation. According to Project Maji’s 10th-anniversary account, the project has served 126 million litres of clean water to more than 380,000 people. Its journey from one solar-powered kiosk to a water initiative marks a decade of expansion.How one puddle in Ghana led to Sunil Lalvani’s Project MajiProject Maji began after a troubling sight in Ghana. The organisation says founder and CEO Sunil Lalvani saw two children drinking water from a puddle in 2015. With a background in electronics, he responded by deploying the project’s first solar-powered water kiosk. Project Maji describes this as the beginning of its work to provide clean water through solar-powered systems. The organisation’s separate account of its history says the first installation opened in Atintan, Ghana, in March 2015 and provided clean water to 1,200 people. The initiative initially operated as a CSR project under Lalvani’s family business.Project Maji reached 126 million litres in 10 yearsA decade after that first installation, Project Maji reports a much larger reach. On its 10th-anniversary page, the organisation says it had served 126,000,000 litres of clean water to more than 380,000 people. The figure covers the organisation’s work across the communities it serves, rather than describing only the original Ghanaian kiosk. Project Maji says its anniversary in 2025 marked 10 years of work, while its current site describes the organisation as a not-for-profit social enterprise. Its stated approach centres on providing continuous access to clean, safe drinking water through solar-powered, technology-enabled systems in rural communities.Solar-powered kiosks became the foundation of its modelProject Maji’s model is built around solar-powered water infrastructure designed for rural communities. The organisation says it works particularly with remote communities of fewer than 1,000 people and aims to provide continuous, reliable access to clean and safe drinking water. Its systems have developed beyond the original kiosk. Project Maji says it later introduced modular kiosks, digital payments and remote monitoring, while its MajiPlus system uses multiple access points connected to one central water source. These developments reflect the organisation’s effort to build water infrastructure that can be maintained and expanded rather than relying solely on a traditional water point.The project expanded beyond GhanaThe 10-year milestone also reflects Project Maji’s expansion beyond Ghana. The organisation says it began operations in Ghana in 2015, expanded to Kenya and started work in Uganda by the end of 2022. UNESCO lists Ghana, Kenya and Uganda among its operating countries. Project Maji’s stated long-term goal is to provide continuous, reliable access to clean, safe drinking water to one million people across rural communities. articles.title: Mali 2014 crash: Families welcome guilty verdict for Swiftair in French court
articles.summary: Relatives of the victims tell the BBC they are relieved to finally have a ruling 12 years after the crash.
articles.body:
Relatives of victims of the 2014 Air Algérie crash have welcomed a Paris court ruling finding Spanish airline Swiftair guilty of involuntary manslaughter.

Sandrine Tricot, who lost her husband Frederic Tricot in the crash, told the BBC it was a relief to finally have a verdict after "4,449 days of waiting for the victims' families".

The French court on Monday fined the airline €225,000 ($256,000; £193,000), the maximum penalty, over the crash that killed all 116 people on board flight AH5017 from the Burkina Faso capital, Ouagadougou, to Algeria's main airport in Algiers.

Swiftair's defence rejected the French investigation, describing the case as "a botched job".

Spanish prosecutors had previously closed their own investigation without bringing any charges.

The court said "negligence" in Swiftair's training had "certainly contributed to the accident".

The McDonnell Douglas MD-83, owned by Swiftair and leased to Air Algérie with its crew, crashed in northern Mali on 24 July 2014.

Those killed included 54 French citizens, 23 Burkinabè nationals, as well as Lebanese and Algerian passengers and six Spanish crew members.

The crash happened as the aircraft flew through a storm in the semi-arid Sahel region, south of the Sahara Desert.

Investigators found that the anti-icing system had not been activated, causing ice crystals to form on pressure sensors. This led to an automatic reduction in engine power and the subsequent crash.

The trial opened in Paris in March, more than 12 years after the disaster.

Nathalie Police, who lost her 65-year-old father Didier and her 18-year-old half-brother Nicolas, attended the entire four-week trial.

Outside the court on Monday, she stood alongside Tricot. Both welcomed the ruling.

"The amount of money was never the end goal. We are relieved that justice has finally been delivered," Tricot told the BBC.

"No amount of money could bring back our loved ones."

Tricot heads the French national federation for victims of terrorist attacks and collective accidents, which joined the case as a civil party.

She said it had been difficult to coordinate with families in Algeria and Burkina Faso who also lost relatives, but hoped the ruling would bring them some peace.

"The conviction is an important step towards recognising criminal responsibility for the disaster."

Sébastien Busy, a lawyer representing most of the victims, described the conviction as a relief. He said Swiftair would also have to cover legal costs, which could exceed the €225,000 fine.

articles.title: Seoul summons Ukraine envoy, demands apology after Zelenskyy reveals North Korean POW transfer
articles.summary: Seoul called for an official apology from Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed, what it says was a secret transfer of two North Korean
articles.body: Seoul called for an official apology from Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed, what it says was a secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.Zelenskyy revealed to the UN General Assembly last week that the soldiers were captured on a battlefield between Russia and Ukraine in early 2025, and that Ukraine had delivered them to South Korea. Thousands of North Korean soldiers, including the two, have been dispatched to aid Russia in its conflict with Ukraine.Lee Jae Myung, the president of South Korea, immediately accused Ukraine of breaking a nondisclosure agreement over the transfer. Ukraine denies entering into such an agreement.Seong Ghi-hong, Lee's senior presidential public relations advisor, voiced "strong regret" at Ukraine's recent actions late on Sunday and called for an official apology and justification.Andrii Vieshkin, the ambassador of Ukraine to Seoul, was summoned by the South Korean Foreign Ministry on Monday to protest what it called Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the inmates' transfer, and its false denial that the two nations had agreed to keep the matter quiet.According to a statement from the ministry, Vieshkin promised to communicate Seoul's stance to his administration. The Ukrainian Embassy in Seoul did not respond to repeated demands for comment.Seong said that Ukraine’s “false” denial of the nondisclosure agreement was “an act that seriously undermines trust between the two governments and causes significant damage to friendly relations between the two countries.”According to Seong, the arrangement was achieved because Kyiv was afraid about potential political backlash for losing the chance to trade them for Ukrainian troops detained in Russia, while Seoul was anxious about the safety of the North Korean soldiers, and their families in the North.POWs from North Korea desired to relocate to South Korea.The two troops stated in interviews with the media that they intended to relocate to South Korea while they were still in Ukraine.Seoul has urged Ukraine to refrain from returning them to North Korea, where they may be persecuted. The South has a policy of welcoming and providing financial help to North Korean defectors, and it officially views the North as part of its territory.Since the end of the 1950–53 Korean war, over 34,000 North Koreans have escaped to South Korea, primarily in the previous three decades. The majority were female citizens from the impoverished northern regions of the North. Soldiers seldom defect.Zelenskyy stated in his statement to the United Nations that "one of them attempted suicide, when he knew he was going to be captured", and was taken aback by that. He was spared death by fate. In the North, individuals are raised in this manner.According to some observers, Zelenskyy probably chose to highlight the threat posed by North Korea's involvement in the conflict in order to secure greater support from the West.The liberal administration of South Korea, meantime, was concerned that the transfer's announcement may incite a furious reaction from the North, and undermine attempts to restore diplomatic relations between Washington and Pyongyang.South Korea has declined to provide Ukraine with direct military assistance.Since Russia's invasion in 2022, South Korea, a rising arms exporter with a well-equipped, and US-backed military, has joined US-led economic sanctions against Russia, and given humanitarian supplies and other support to Ukraine.However, in keeping with a long-standing policy of not delivering weapons to nations actively involved in combat, Seoul has rejected pleas from Kyiv and NATO to offer direct military help to Ukraine.In April 2025, North Korea and Russia acknowledged that their armed forces had engaged in joint combat to thwart a Ukrainian invasion of Russia's Kursk border area. According to South Korea, the US, and others, North Korea has also given Russia missiles, artillery, and ammunition in exchange for military and economic support.According to South Korea's spy agency, 2,000 of the approximately 15,000 personnel that North Korea supplied were killed last year.Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, has been able to more assertively pursue a nuclear weapons development, and resist pressure from the United States by increasing collaboration with Russia.In an apparent attempt to resume diplomatic relations with Kim, US President Donald Trump reduced a military exercise with South Korea this month. However, North Korea has stated that this action was insufficient to persuade it to resume negotiations.In protest of Kyiv's revelation of the transfer of arrested North Korean troops to South Korea, South Korea's foreign ministry called Ukraine's acting ambassador on Monday, and requested an official apology and explanation.Despite what Seoul claimed was a clear agreement between the two nations to keep the matter confidential, the ministry said it had called in acting ambassador Andrii Vieshkin, and expressed deep regret that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy made the disclosure at the UN General Assembly.According to a statement from the ministry, South Korea also objected over what it deemed a misleading statement made by the Ukrainian presidential office denying the existence of such a confidentiality agreement, and asked Kyiv to take action to stop a repeat."First Vice Minister Park Yoon-joo stressed that the disclosure of a falsehood that there was no confidential agreement seriously undermines trust between the two governments and is an action that can cause problems for friendly ties," added.According to South Korean media, Kyiv stated that the idea to make the move public was understood.You use AI every day.
