articles.title: A California family donated its historic 390-acre ranch to Cal Poly after 150 years of farming; the protected property includes 100 acres of prime irrigated soil, four wells and a seven-acre reservoir
articles.summary: After 150 years of farming, the Brughelli family has donated its historic 390-acre ranch in San Luis Obispo County to Cal Poly.
articles.body: After 150 years of farming, the Brughelli family has donated its historic 390-acre ranch in San Luis Obispo County to Cal Poly. The property, located just south of the county’s regional airport, will become a living classroom where students can study agriculture, conservation, water management and natural-resource stewardship. According to Cal Poly’s announcement, Brughelli Ranch contains 100 acres of irrigated Class I soil, four interconnected wells and a seven-acre reservoir, along with dry-farming and additional plantable acreage. The land is already protected by an agricultural conservation easement and enrolled in the Williamson Act, ensuring that its agricultural identity will continue. The gift also preserves a family legacy that began with Aurelio Brughelli’s work on the ranch in 1928 and continued through generations of farming, land care and community involvement.A working ranch with a long historyBrughelli Ranch is not an empty tract waiting to be developed. It is a working agricultural property with a history stretching back 150 years.The ranch’s documented story began with a United States government land patent acquired by John Anderson in July 1875. William Buckley later owned the property, followed by Dave McKeen around 1882.Aurelio Brughelli began working on the ranch in 1928 and acquired it about two decades later from the McKeen estate. His connection to the land became the foundation of the family’s long relationship with the property.Aurelio’s son, Ercole Charles Brughelli, was born on the ranch in 1928. He grew up there and remained connected to it for the rest of his life.After serving in the United States Army during the Korean War, where he received a Purple Heart, Ercole returned to the family farm. He later married Naomie Jones in 1965, and the couple managed the ranch for roughly four decades, as per the report.From family land to university propertyThe Brughelli Estate donated the property to Cal Poly after the deaths of Naomie in 2008 and Ercole in 2023.The family trustees continued managing the ranchland before deciding that Cal Poly was the right institution to carry its agricultural and conservation legacy into the future.Mark Amos, a Brughelli trustee, said the family believed the university was the clear choice when it came time to protect the land’s future. He expressed hope that Cal Poly students would learn on the ranch and take that knowledge into their careers.The donation changes the ownership of the land while preserving much of its purpose. The ranch will remain connected to agriculture rather than becoming a residential or commercial development.For Cal Poly, the gift provides hundreds of acres near campus where students can apply classroom lessons in a real working environment. For the Brughelli family, it creates a way for the property to continue serving future generations.The value of prime soilAbout 60 per cent of Brughelli Ranch is classified by the United States Department of Agriculture as prime agricultural land.The property includes 100 acres of irrigated Class I soils, which are considered among the most productive agricultural soils. These fields can support a broad range of crops when sufficient water and suitable management are available.The northern part of the ranch contains irrigated cropland. Dry-farm and additional plantable acreage extend south and west across gently rolling terrain.The difference between irrigated and dry-farmed land is important in California. Irrigation provides more control over crop production, while dry farming depends more heavily on seasonal rainfall and soil moisture.The availability of both types of land gives the ranch educational value. Students can compare different agricultural systems, examine water requirements and study how soil, weather and management affect crop production.Existing leases with established farming operators will continue to support agricultural operations on the land. Those leases also provide a revenue base for managing the property.Water resources on the propertyBrughelli Ranch includes four interconnected wells and a seven-acre reservoir.Water is one of the most important resources on any California farm. A reliable water system can determine what crops can be grown, how much land can be cultivated and how resilient a farm is during dry periods.The ranch’s water infrastructure creates opportunities for students and researchers to examine groundwater, surface storage, irrigation systems and water conservation.The property is also crossed by San Luis Creek and Buckley Creek. These waterways add ecological features to a landscape that is otherwise shaped by agriculture.Creeks can provide habitat, move water through the property and influence soil and vegetation. They also create opportunities to study the relationship between farming and natural-resource protection.Managing a working farm near waterways requires careful attention to runoff, erosion, nutrient movement and water quality. Those issues are central to modern agriculture, especially in regions where water supplies are under pressure.The wells, reservoir and creeks therefore make the ranch more than a collection of fields. They form a working water system that can be studied in real time.Protected by a conservation easementThe property was permanently protected through an agricultural conservation easement established in 2015.The easement was created by the Ercole and Naomie Brughelli Trust in partnership with the city of San Luis Obispo and the Land Conservancy of San Luis Obispo County. It limits development and protects the agricultural and natural features of the ranch.The land is also enrolled in the Williamson Act, a California programme that supports the long-term preservation of agricultural and open space land by placing restrictions on development.These protections were in place before Cal Poly received the donation. That means the university acquired land with a legally established conservation identity.The easement will guide how Cal Poly manages the ranch. The university must respect the terms of the agreement, the Williamson Act, the family’s intentions and its own educational mission.Permanent protection is important because ownership can change. A university may manage the property differently from a private family, but the conservation easement ensures that the ranch’s agricultural future remains protected.A living classroom for studentsCal Poly is known for its Learn by Doing approach.The Brughelli Ranch expands that philosophy by giving students access to a productive agricultural landscape where classroom concepts can be tested through direct experience.Agriculture students may study crop production, soil health, irrigation and farm business management. Environmental science students may examine creeks, habitats and conservation practices. Engineering students could explore water infrastructure, equipment and agricultural technology.Researchers may also collaborate with growers, industry partners and local organisations on practical problems facing California agriculture.A living classroom offers advantages that a laboratory cannot fully reproduce. Students can observe changing conditions across seasons, see how weather affects crops and understand the decisions required to manage land under real economic and environmental pressures.They also learn that agriculture is connected to water, soil, biodiversity, markets and communities. A working ranch makes those relationships visible.Conservation and agriculture togetherThe donation demonstrates that productive farmland and conservation do not have to be opposing goals.Agricultural land can provide food, income and research opportunities while also supporting natural features such as creeks, mature vegetation and wildlife habitat.The challenge is to manage those uses responsibly. Farming can affect water quality and soil health, but conservation practices can reduce erosion, improve soil structure and protect waterways.Students working at Brughelli Ranch may be able to study practices such as cover cropping, efficient irrigation, buffer zones and soil monitoring. The property’s existing conservation protections can provide a framework for testing methods that support both production and environmental stewardship.Cal Poly President Jeffrey D. Armstrong said the ranch would give students a place where agriculture, conservation and natural-resource stewardship come together.That combination reflects the realities facing California. Farmers must produce food while responding to drought, changing weather, soil degradation and pressure from development.The role of family stewardshipThe ranch’s future is connected to the work of several generations.Aurelio Brughelli began working on the property in 1928. Ercole returned to the ranch after military service and spent decades managing it with Naomie. The family did not treat the land simply as a financial asset. It was also a home, workplace and community responsibility.The couple often worked with local young people interested in agriculture and the environment. That experience adds another dimension to the donation.The ranch had already been functioning as a place of informal learning before it became connected with Cal Poly. Students and young people could see how agricultural work was carried out and how land was cared for over time.The university can build on that tradition through formal classes, research projects and public programmes.The family’s legacy is therefore preserved not only in the property’s name or history but in its continued use as a place where people learn about working landscapes.A bridge between past and futureThe donation creates a connection between traditional farming knowledge and modern agricultural research.The Brughelli family’s experience reflects practical knowledge developed through decades of observation and work. Cal Poly brings students, faculty, scientific tools and partnerships with agricultural industries.Those forms of knowledge can strengthen each other. Researchers may test new ideas, while farmers provide insight into what works under local conditions.A university-owned working ranch can also serve as a place to evaluate technology before it is applied elsewhere. Irrigation monitoring, crop trials, soil analysis and conservation systems can be studied under real conditions.The property’s location near campus makes regular access easier for students and faculty. It can become a long-term resource rather than an occasional field-trip destination.That continuity matters. Agriculture changes across seasons and years, so ongoing observation can produce more useful information than a single short study.Cal Poly’s agricultural holdingsCal Poly already manages extensive agricultural land.The university maintains more than 10,000 acres, making it the largest university agricultural landholder in California and one of the largest university landowners in the United States. Its holdings include campus and nearby agricultural lands, Swanton Pacific Ranch in Santa Cruz County and Cal Poly Solano Campus in Vallejo.The Brughelli Ranch adds another important property close to the San Luis Obispo campus.Its productive soils, water resources and protected status complement Cal Poly’s broader mission. The ranch can support teaching and research while remaining part of the region’s working agricultural landscape.The new property may also allow the university to expand collaborations with local farmers, environmental organisations and government agencies.Because the university already has experience managing agricultural lands, it is positioned to incorporate the ranch into existing programmes while respecting its distinct history and conservation requirements.A gift with lasting valueThe Brughelli family’s donation gives Cal Poly access to a property that combines history, productivity and environmental significance.The 390 acres include prime irrigated soils, dry-farm land, plantable acreage, four interconnected wells, a seven-acre reservoir and two creeks. The land has supported agriculture for 150 years and is protected against development through a conservation easement and the Williamson Act.Its value cannot be measured only by the size of the donation. The ranch provides a setting where students can learn how agriculture operates in the real world and how conservation can be integrated into productive landscapes.The gift also prevents the property from becoming disconnected from its agricultural identity. Future students will encounter fields, water systems and natural features that were cared for by the Brughelli family across generations.For the family, donating the ranch ensures that its future remains active rather than frozen. The land will continue to grow crops, support research, teach students and contribute to the stewardship of California’s working landscapes.What began as a family farm in the 19th century will now serve as a university classroom for generations to come.You use AI every day. articles.title: Is Rohit Sharma injured before IND vs WI 2nd ODI? Viral video shows veteran Indian opener slip on team bus stairs
articles.summary: The health status of Rohit Sharma has come under scrutiny after the former India
articles.body:
Rohit Sharma slipped while stepping off the team bus after India's win in the 1st ODI on Sunday night.

The BCCI has not reported any injury or fitness concern.

The 2nd ODI is on Wednesday in Guwahati, with India leading the series 1-0.

Rohit Sharma suffers an injury scare right after India wins the first ODI against the West Indies

India's win in the first ODI against the West Indies was built on Virat Kohli's unbeaten 139 and Shubman Gill's 110. Chasing 296, the hosts finished the job with 50 balls to spare. Hours later, a different clip took over social media. It showed Rohit Sharma losing his footing on the team bus stairs.

The incident happened on Sunday night, as the squad returned to its hotel in Thiruvananthapuram. Rohit was helped to his feet quickly, and no injury has been reported so far. Even so, the video has raised an obvious question ahead of Wednesday's second ODI, and fans have not stopped asking it.

Rohit is 39 and plays only ODIs for India. Every fitness scare now matters more, with the 2027 World Cup just a year away and his place in the side still discussed after every series. Here is what happened on the bus and what it could mean for Guwahati.

What happened to Rohit Sharma on the team bus?

India's chase in Thiruvananthapuram ended with Kohli hitting the winning runs, and the players headed back to the team hotel to celebrate. When the bus pulled up, the squad began stepping off one by one. Rohit was coming down the last few stairs when his foot slipped and he lost his balance .

He was seen slipping through the stairs, ending up near the entrance of the bus. Support staff and police personnel standing nearby rushed forward at once, and he was back on his feet quickly. The video has since been circulating on social media, with fans concerned that the Hitman may have suffered an injury from this misstep.

Is Rohit Sharma injured ahead of the 2nd ODI?

There is no official word of any injury. The BCCI and Rohit himself have not reported any injury, and no fitness update has been issued. Reports so far describe it as a scare rather than an injury. Until the team says otherwise, that remains the working assumption. Rohit had a quieter night with the bat in the opener.

He was dismissed in the 32, and Kohli and Gill then put together a big partnership, with both bringing up centuries. India lead the three-match series 1-0, and Rohit will be looking for a bigger score in Guwahati. India's camp has already dealt with plenty of fitness problems this year.

Against that backdrop, even a minor scare involving a senior player stands out. However, for now, the evidence points to a scare rather than an injury. If Rohit opens in Guwahati on Wednesday, fans will soon forget the clip. If he does not, the questions about his fitness will resurface, and they will be louder a year out from a World Cup.

articles.summary: Tripura ADC Village Committee polls see 75% turnout, largely peaceful; CPM alleges irregularities, BJP rejects. Voting held for 4,597 posts; counting Oct 5.
articles.body: Agartala: Tripura’s ADC Village Committee elections passed off largely peacefully on Monday, with the State Election Commission (SEC) reporting around 75% turnout, which could rise as voters remained in queues after polling closed.SEC secretary Anurag Sen said there were no major incidents, while CPM alleged fraudulent voting, obstruction of candidates and polling agents and difficulties accessing booths in parts of West Tripura and Sepahijala.Radhacharan Debbarma, senior CPM neta and former ADC CEM, claimed opposition polling agents were barred from several booths.BJP dismissed the allegations as baseless. The SEC said prompt actions was taken whenever disturbances were reported.Polling was held across 587 committees for 4,597 positions in 2,634 constituencies. articles.title: Nepal flood- When the mountain fell:  The warning no one could read in time

articles.body: August 26th, 2026 began like any other morning along the Trishuli River — until, without a monsoon downpour, without a forecast, without any conventional trigger at all, a mountain gave way. High on the Nepal-China border in Rasuwa district, a mass of ice and rock sheared off and plunged into the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor. Within thirty minutes, according to a report shared by ICIMOD, water levels on the Trishuli River had risen by as much as nine metres. The surge tore through the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal frontier and struck dozens of settlements along a 72-kilometre stretch of river, choking hydropower intakes with debris, jamming tunnels that were the economic lifeline of the valley, and leaving thousands of lives unaccounted for.By UN Nepal's Situation Report 8 (15 September), the toll stood at 1,399 confirmed dead, 5,179 still missing, and 13,742 rescued. NDRRMA's(National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority) Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment recorded 7,570 damaged buildings — concentrated in Nuwakot — alongside 41 bridges washed away entirely, 15 hydropower projects damaged across Rasuwa and Nuwakot (including 93 workers missing at Rasuwagadhi alone), and only 3 of the three districts' schools left standing safely enough for students to return. Roads, water systems, health posts and government offices across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading remain disrupted, and that damage isn't incidental to the response — it is actively constraining humanitarian access to the hardest-hit, hardest-to-reach villages even now.The scale of loss is the story everyone has already told. The more consequential story — is what happened, or failed to happen, in the hours and weeks before the mountain fell: what the satellites could see, what the institutions could act on, and where the gap between the two turned a geological event into a mass-casualty disaster.The warning that arrived too quietlyIt turns out the mountain had been moving for months. A Nature News Q&A (2 September 2026) reported that analysis of European Space Agency Sentinel-1 radar data (a collection of high-resolution, all-weather, day-and-night images of the Earth's surface), covering 8 January through 18 August 2026, found the glacier-rock mass creeping downhill at roughly 10 millimetres per month in the weeks before collapse. In hindsight, that is a signature: a slope in the final stages of failure. In real time, it was almost useless.That gap is the crux of the problem. Ten millimetres of monthly creep is the kind of signal that shows up clearly in a retrospective satellite time series and almost nowhere in an operational early-warning workflow — existing monitoring techniques still struggle to convert "acceleration" into an actionable, dated forecast of imminent failure.The instability sat directly on, or near, the Nepal-Tibet border, in terrain where effective early warning depends on rapid, routine observation-sharing between the two countries — sharing that, by every account of this event, did not functionally exist. So even where the data existed, the institutional pipeline to turn it into a downstream evacuation order may not exist. This is worth noting, because it reframes the disaster: not as an unforeseeable act of nature, but as a hazard that was partially visible, moving through a governance and monitoring architecture that had no mechanism to translate visibility into warning.A mountain that had been warming for decadesThe climate dimension of the story is easy to narrate and just as easily dismissed too quickly — the real picture sits in between. Data compiled and analysed by “The Climate Brink”( shows that summer temperatures at the collapse site have warmed by around 0.29°C per decade since 1940, with the most recent thirty years (1996–2025) running roughly 1°C above the 1961–1990 baseline. The four most recent summers — 2022 through 2025 — all rank among the five warmest on record at the site. The collapse came at the tail of an exceptionally hot stretch: July 2026 was the second-warmest in an 86-year record, and the first three weeks of August ran hotter than any complete August ever recorded there, before the mountain gave way on the 26th.None of this means a warm summer, by itself, brings a mountain down. What sustained warmth does is quieter and more structural: it melts the ice that buttresses steep slopes, sends meltwater into rock fractures, and degrades the permafrost(any ground that remains completely frozen — 32°F (0°C) or colder — for at least two years straight). That acts as a frozen adhesive holding fractured high-altitude rock together. Layer onto that a longer-term signal — regional glacier mass balance has been declining for decades, with estimates putting cumulative ice-area loss in this catchment above 40% — and you have a slope that has been losing its structural support system incrementally for years, even if no single year "caused" the collapse.So can this event be attributed to climate change? The thinning of Himalayan ice is not new, and hazard from these slopes is driven less by “how much” ice sits on them than by “how fast” the ice and the frozen ground beneath it are changing. A cold glacier frozen stably to its bed is comparatively secure; one in active transition — warming, thinning, losing its permafrost cement — is not. What can be said with confidence is that the mountain failed inside a climate trend, not despite one: temperatures at the site are rising, the glacier's structural support is eroding, and that combination is precisely the kind of long-run vulnerability that turns an otherwise geologically plausible event into a more probable one. Formal attribution of this single collapse to climate change would require the kind of detailed forensic reconstruction that, for comparable events like the 2021 Chamoli disaster, took scientists a year or more to complete — so any confident claim in either direction, made this soon, should be treated with some scepticism.The question that should outlast the news cycleStrip away the individual numbers and a pattern emerges that should matter more to policymakers than any single death toll: a partially observable hazard, on a slope that had been destabilising for decades, in a transboundary zone with no functioning mechanism to convert satellite data into a warning a villager downstream could act on. That is not a story about an unpredictable mountain. It is a story about the distance between what modern remote sensing can see and what modern institutions are built to do with it — and about how that distance, in this case, was measured in over a thousand lives. The rebuilding conversation in Nepal will inevitably center on roads, bridges and hydropower. It should. But the harder, less visible reconstruction task is the one this event has exposed most starkly: an early-warning architecture that can survive a border, act on a ten-millimetre-a-month signal, and reach a valley faster than a flood can travel through it.What Comes Next: The scale of this disaster means the response cannot be sequential — search and rescue, relief, and reconstruction planning have to run in parallel, each on its own clock.Immediate: With 5,179 people still unaccounted for as of the 15 September situation report, search and rescue cannot be allowed to wind down on the same timeline as the media cycle. Every day that passes narrows the odds of finding survivors, but it does not reduce the humanitarian obligation to find the dead.Immediate to short-term: Stabilising livelihoods·Cash compensation to affected families should follow quickly, and it should be understood for what it is and isn't. It will not offset a life lost or a home destroyed — no transfer does that — but it buys families the one thing a disaster strips away first: the ability to make near-term decisions (food, temporary shelter, transport, medicine) without going into debt to do it.·Alongside cash relief, near-zero-interest soft loans from nationalised banks, disbursed on an expedited basis to residents of the affected districts, would let households restart the smaller economic activities — shops, farming inputs, transport, small trades — that a lump-sum grant alone can't fully restore.Short-term: ·Reconstruction of the 41 washed-out bridges, repair of damaged roads and transport links, and desilting of the Trishuli and its tributaries should begin as soon as safety assessments allow, both because isolated villages need physical reconnection and because a silted, debris-choked riverbed raises the flood risk for the next monsoon before the region has even recovered from this one.Medium to long-term: Financing The World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and JICA all have existing disaster-recovery and resilient-infrastructure financing instruments suited to exactly this kind of multi-sector reconstruction. "Build back better" has to mean something concrete here — hydropower and settlements re-sited or re-engineered with a wider margin from the riverbank, construction standards that account for debris-flow and flash-flood loading rather than just seismic loading, and coordination across the many stakeholders (government ministries, donors, local governments, communities.An early-warning system that actually worksClosing that gap requires two things operating together, not separately: formal, routine institution-to-institution data-sharing across the Nepal-China border, so that monitoring doesn't stop at a national boundary the hazard itself ignores; and active community-level participation in the last mile of that system, so that a warning issued in a monitoring center actually becomes an evacuation on the ground in time to matter.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.
